extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, law students, and litigators working on patent infringement/validity disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the treatment, admissibility, weight, and limits of expert testimony and documentary evidence in patent litigation, and on the evidentiary effect of an issued patent. Aimed at resolving questions of novelty, infringement, construction, and proof in court and jury proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of patent-expert testimony (partisan role)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent-expert is not a judge; he is commonly partisan and his testimony is expected to support the claims of the litigant who presents him. His opinion is received in evidence only in connection with the reasons on which it is based, and is to be accepted or rejected by the jury according to their own view of its fallacy or truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ascribe judicial functions to the patent-expert or demand freedom from partisanship. The expert's relation to the jury is like counsel to the court: pointing out facts and applying them in support of claims. Their statements of fact and opinions are to be weighed like those of other witnesses; their opinions are followed when, in the judgment of the jury, they are supported by the facts from which they are deduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury's role in resolving conflicting expert opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: When experts differ, the jury (or the trier of fact) must decide which opinions are correct after considering the reasons given, examination of models and other evidence, and by exercising its own judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert opinions are 'merely' opinions; the jury should consider the experts' reasons, inspect models, deliberately exercise their own judgments, and then decide. Courts may instruct juries on the rules to consider when submitting expert evidence under general instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two classes of patent experts: scientific experts
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific expert is one who, by study or experiments, is familiar with the principles of a science and qualified to understand, distinguish, and explain properties of objects pertaining to that science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific experts are appropriate on questions including: (1) whether an alleged invention is the result of an inventive act; (2) whether elements described are essential to the idea of means; (3) whether a given invention embraces or excludes another; (4) whether a given invention is substantially the same in principle, function, or effect with another. They bring broad knowledge of fundamental truths, chemistry/physics, progress of arts, and tests to distinguish means/ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two classes of patent experts: mechanical experts
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanical expert is a practical artisan who, by training, has acquired skill in rules and manipulations enabling him to comprehend and apply instruments and methods of an art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical experts represent the skilled workman and are important for assessing: usefulness of an invention, the ability of artisans to reproduce it from the disclosure, sufficiency of prior descriptions in novelty defenses, alleged inutility, and whether a specification furnishes necessary guidance. They evaluate practicability and performance in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single witness may testify in both scientific and mechanical capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Although scientific and mechanical experts occupy distinct spheres, the same person may appear and testify in both capacities if he possesses the required skill and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the witness truly has both the scientific knowledge and practical training, courts may admit testimony in either or both roles; qualification is fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of expert testimony — scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions of experts, with their reasons, are admissible on questions for the court as well as those for the jury, provided the subject-matter is one to which such evidence can properly be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction of a patent is principally for the judge (a matter of law), but the court may avail itself of expert evidence to the extent it deems expedient; neither party has an absolute right to offer expert evidence and the judge may refuse to admit it. If the judge's construction shows no infringement or invalidity, there is no occasion for extraneous evidence and the court may direct verdict for defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts cannot determine legal questions or override established facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert opinions that purport to state questions of law, or to decide legal construction of a patent, are not proper for juries and have no force except as they embrace factual matters. Experts are not permitted to prevail over results of practical operation, experiment, or necessary inferences from established facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an expert's opinion includes legal conclusions (e.g., construction of a patent), that portion is not for the jury. Courts and juries must reject expert statements contrary to demonstrable experimental results or established facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for evaluating expert evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert evidence is judged by the same standards as ordinary evidence: its value depends on the skill, credibility, reasons, and factual basis of the expert, not merely on number of experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert evidence based on facts prevails over one based on mere theories. The weight of expert testimony is measured by the reasons they embody; practitioners should prefer well-reasoned, fact-supported expert opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's use of independent experts when experts disagree
rubrics_metrics.description: When scientific evidence conflicts, the court may employ an independent expert to advise as to the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have discretion to call or consult independent experts to resolve technical disputes; this is particularly appropriate where the court cannot form its own opinion on recondite scientific matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary documentary evidence in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal documentary evidence includes Patent Office files and records, the patent in dispute (if regular on its face), other patents (domestic or foreign) when duly verified, specifications, drawings, and models, and private agreements such as assignments, grants, and licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are admissible if regular on their face even without recitals of prerequisites. Other patents must be appropriately authenticated. Specifications, drawings, and models attached to patents are admissible if legally authenticated. Assignments/grants/licenses show title or authority to make/use/sell. Use certified/sealed copies where statute requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and use of caveats, disclaimers, applications, and correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveats, disclaimers, the patent application, and correspondence with the Patent Office may be admitted for limited purposes: to prove the claimant's ideas at a date, to show abandonment, or to define the nature/scope/meaning of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caveat may be offered to prove the inventor's claims at the date of transmission to the Patent Office (but not perfection). A disclaimer (signed/filed) is admissible on abandonment or scope-limiting issues. Application materials and Patent Office correspondence may be produced as declarations accompanying an act and to define what the inventor meant by his claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary papers by third parties generally inadmissible (hearsay) but useful to fix dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary papers filed by third parties in the Patent Office are generally inadmissible as res inter alios acta and hearsay, though they may sometimes be received to fix a date or describe attributes of an invention whose existence is otherwise established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such papers cautiously: they are not competent evidence of inventorship or primary facts, but may help establish chronology or corroborate established facts where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and evidentiary weight of Patent Office certified copies and foreign patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Certified copies of Patent Office records, patents, and certified copies of foreign patents (properly authenticated) are admissible and by statute are prima facie evidence of the matters they contain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provisions render copies of Patent Office records and duly authenticated patents prima facie evidence. Copies of foreign patents deposited in the Patent Office sufficiently show dates and numbers. Clerks and officers of the Patent Office may be proper witnesses to prove file contents. Incorrect transcripts may be corrected by new transcripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and role of models, drawings, and file-wrapper
rubrics_metrics.description: Models, drawings, and the file-wrapper and correspondence attached to the Patent Office file are admissible and may be examined to determine scope, mode of operation, and transactions between inventor and Office; rejected specifications/drawings may still be relevant when considered with perfected adaptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models and drawings can be admitted as evidence of the invention's attributes. File-wrapper contents can aid interpretation of the patent and may be examined to determine the scope of a re-issue. Rejected or preliminary drawings may help fix dates or show inventor's design when later perfected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence of validity and limits of its conclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent, regular on its face, is prima facie evidence of all facts essential to its own validity and will prevail unless overcome by clear evidence that removes all reasonable doubt; however, issuance of a patent is not conclusive proof of validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To defeat a patent, evidence must remove all reasonable doubt. While statutory presumptions give weight to patents and Patent Office records, courts may set aside patents when clear, convincing contrary evidence exists. Certified copies of patents/specifications serve as prima facie proof of particulars of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of documentary evidence to show title, authority, and transaction history
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments, grants, licenses, and other private writings are competent to show title to the patented invention and authority conferred on defendants; file-wrapper and Patent Office correspondence may be used to show transactions between inventor and the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private writings follow ordinary rules of admissibility (authentication, originals/certified copies, business records exceptions). Some classes of corporate or third-party records may be inadmissible against a party unless foundation or privity is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: When court may decide factual questions without expert evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court's interpretation of the patent demonstrates no infringement, or that the patent is void for want of novelty, or that a re-issue cannot legitimately be construed to amend the original, then extraneous expert evidence is unnecessary and the court should direct a verdict accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In clear cases the court may feel no need for an expert to explain terms of art or patent descriptions and can treat identity/diversity as a jury question only under general instructions; the court may set aside unsatisfactory verdicts against the weight of evidence.
